title: Why does only the longest side need checking?
description: For the lengths six, seven and twelve, the longest side is compared with the other two added together, and the other two comparisons are shown to hold without effort. Keeko doubts the need for the longest side and says any one comparison is enough.
teaching_notes: One idea: the comparison that matters is the one for the longest side, because the other two comparisons always hold. Watch for children who check a shorter side and stop, as that comparison holds even when no triangle exists.

source: Check the lengths 6, 7 and 12 by comparing only the longest length with the sum of the other two, and then check the other two comparisons to see that they hold.
video_script.why: The child has seen that a triangle exists when the circles cross and now learns why one comparison, for the longest side, is enough.
video_script.substitution: The longest length is twelve and the other two lengths are six and seven, which add to thirteen.
video_script.anchor: Three lengths of six, seven and twelve, with the longest marked
video_script.wrong_move: A child checks a shorter side against the other two, sees that it holds, and stops, though that comparison holds even when no triangle exists.
video_script.payoff_line: Twelve is less than thirteen, and that is the only check needed.

final_answer.value: 12 < 13 is the only check needed; the lengths 6, 7 and 12 pass
final_answer.spoken: twelve is less than thirteen, and that is the only check needed, so the lengths six, seven and twelve pass

never_show: the words only check needed before the answer beat
maths_rules: 6 < 7 + 12 = 19 and 7 < 6 + 12 = 18, both hold because 12 is already bigger than 6 and than 7
so one comparison, for the longest side, decides the matter
counter-example: 3, 4, 8: 3 < 4 + 8 = 12 holds, but 8 > 3 + 4 = 7, so no triangle
video_script.design: One idea: only the comparison for the longest side can fail. Three lengths and three comparisons; Keeko's doubt closes the video.

beats.on_screen: title card Which Check Matters?; strips of 6 cm, 7 cm and 12 cm beside a question mark

marks.ask: the strips of six, seven and twelve slide in

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>Check the lengths six, seven and twelve by comparing only the longest length.
<bookmark mark='check'/>Then see whether the other two comparisons hold.

beats.on_screen: the strips and the question mark stay on the board

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: three strips with the longest one marked in red and the other two stacked end to end in yellow

marks.stack: the two shorter strips are stacked end to end
marks.long: the longest strip is marked in red

beats.colours: longest in red, the other two in yellow
narration: <bookmark mark='strips'/>Here are the three lengths as strips.
<bookmark mark='stack'/>Put the two shorter strips end to end.
<bookmark mark='long'/>Then compare them with the longest strip.
<bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the lengths are six, seven and twelve.

beats.on_screen: To find: which comparison matters, and do the lengths pass?
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find which comparison matters, and whether the lengths pass.

marks.others: 6 and 7 are added to 13 in yellow

beats.colours: longest in red, the other two in yellow
narration: <bookmark mark='longest'/>Step one, the longest length is twelve.
<bookmark mark='others'/>The other two add to six plus seven, which is thirteen.

beats.on_screen: Step 2: 12 < 13, so the longest comparison holds

marks.compare: 12 and 13 are written with a less-than sign and a tick

narration: <bookmark mark='compare'/>Step two, twelve is less than thirteen, so this comparison holds.
<bookmark mark='six'/>Step three, six is less than seven plus twelve, which is nineteen.
<bookmark mark='seven'/>Seven is less than six plus twelve, which is eighteen.

beats.on_screen: Step 4: each short length is compared with a sum that contains 12, which is already bigger
narration: <bookmark mark='why'/>Step four, both of those sums contain the length twelve.
Twelve alone is already bigger than six and than seven, so those two comparisons must hold.

beats.on_screen: Answer: 12 < 13 is the only check needed; the lengths 6, 7 and 12 pass
narration: <bookmark mark='ans'/>Twelve is less than thirteen, and that is the only check needed.
That means the lengths six, seven and twelve pass the check.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the three strips
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: the set 3, 4, 8 appears; 3 < 4 + 8 = 12 is ticked; 8 > 3 + 4 = 7 is crossed
beats.colours: tick in green, cross in red
narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks any one comparison is enough.
<bookmark mark='short'/>Try three, four and eight. Three is less than four plus eight, so that comparison holds.
<bookmark mark='long'/>But eight is greater than three plus four, so no triangle exists. Always check the longest side.
